lines.text: What if the man who checks the slot machines is the one rigging them?
In the early nineties, Ron Harris was a computer expert at Nevada's Gaming Control Board.
His job was to find cheating software hidden in casino games.
Agents checked slot machines by plugging in a laptop.
Harris wrote the program on those laptops.
And he hid something inside it.
Every time an agent tested a machine, the program quietly changed it.
Now it paid a jackpot when coins went in a set order.
Only Harris and his friends knew the order.
His friends hit jackpots in Las Vegas, Reno and Lake Tahoe.
Prosecutors could prove at least forty-two thousand dollars.
Nobody knows the real total.
Then he went further.
He built a program that predicted keno numbers without touching the machine at all.
In Las Vegas, he and a partner took ten thousand dollars from a keno machine in under five minutes.
So in January nineteen ninety-five, they flew to Atlantic City.

lines.text: A win that big made the casino suspicious.
Before a cent was paid, the partner was arrested.
Harris was picked up when his plane landed in Las Vegas.
The judge gave him seven years.
"The depth of your betrayal," he said, "was complete."
Today, Harris is in Nevada's Black Book, banned from the casinos he once inspected.
So who checks the people checking the machines?
